item.title: Pawnshops and Property-Related Crime: Lessons from Interwar Tokyo
item.description: arXiv:2610.38365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using ward-level panel data for 1927 to 1935 and fixed-effects models, this study examines how pawnshops were related to property-related crime in interwar Tokyo. Accordingly, public pawnshops targeting low-income borrowers are compared with profit-oriented private pawnshops. The results reveal that public lending is negatively associated with theft and positively associated with fraud and extortion, whereas private lending is negatively associated with fraud and extortion as well as embezzlement. A simple monetization exercise shows that offense counts and victim losses can yield different assessments. Overall, the relationship between credit and crime depended on both institutional design and crime type.
item.dc:creator: Tatsuki Inoue

item.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
item.description: arXiv:2610.38883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects of research studies pre-registered on the AEA RCT Registry and the Open Science Framework. I focus on studies whose results were first publicly released in 2026 and elicit forecasts from models whose training or knowledge cut-off dates were before the relevant set of papers was released. First, LLM models extract forecasting questions from the pre-registrations or pre-analysis plans. These questions elicit forecasted treatment effects; not all resolve in the subsequent papers, but those that do can be used to consider forecast accuracy. Forecasts were elicited for 889 treatment effects from 39 papers with results disclosed in January 2026 or later, or 673 from 33 papers after screening. Forecasts were elicited in raw units but I focus on those that could be standardized and therefore compared across papers. Currently, the median absolute forecast error is 0.054 SD for the best model, the average absolute error is 0.093 SD, and the MSE is 0.0218. The AI forecasts perform substantially better than benchmarks forecasting 0 effect or forecasting the mean effect of other papers' results in that time period. Overall, these results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to be of value in informing policy and research.
item.dc:creator: Eva Vivalt

item.title: Capital growth since the 19th century
item.description: arXiv:2610.38997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We argued in an earlier paper (Getty and Tkachenko 2025b), from data reported for net saving and market-value capital by 94 nations over the period 1980-2021, that net saving has had little or no effect on capital growth at the global scale. Here we extend the study backward to the earliest year, in each country, for which those data have been reported or reconstructed. We find a still smaller margin of possibility (1.6% versus 6.4%) of contribution of net saving to capital growth at the collective scale. We also propose and defend an alternative explanation of capital growth, and suggest a larger role for the cash flow concept in economic analysis.
item.dc:creator: Gordon Getty, Nikita Tkachenko

item.title: Measuring Longer-Horizon Leveraged ETF Performance
item.description: arXiv:2610.39097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many investors hold leveraged exchange-traded funds (LETFs) for more than one day. Because these products reset leverage daily, their longer-horizon returns need not equal the stated leverage multiple times the underlying return. We explain this gap using a return identity that separates what we call the convexity bonus, volatility drag, and product costs. We also discuss several common ways to measure LETF performance and highlight how these measures can produce misleading assessments of how real-world LETFs perform. We propose evaluating ex-post performance using realized terminal wealth, which measures how much invested wealth grew. For ex-ante analysis, we propose using expected log returns to quantify how fast capital compounds over time. We show that estimating expected cumulative return by compounding the historical arithmetic mean can rank investments backwards, report gains for funds that lose money, suggest that infinite leverage is optimal when expected returns exceed borrowing cost, and reward temporary price fluctuations that reduce LETF wealth. We argue that even if the distribution of daily returns is known by the econometrician, expected terminal wealth is sensitive to whether the model draws days independently or draws monthly or annual blocks of daily returns and can be driven by a small number of economically infeasible payouts.
item.dc:creator: Chris Murray, Marco Sammon

item.title: What is Work For? Labor, Politics, and Meaning in the Age of AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.39375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the role of work in providing meaning, purpose, community, and other non-monetary benefits. Using an original cross-national survey of 8,234 working-age adults across the UK, US, Denmark, and India, I study the factors that motivate people in their work, with an eye toward the future AI economic transformation. I find that 81% of respondents report being satisfied with their job, and a majority across all four countries are strongly motivated by the non-monetary components of their employment. Using an original "Work Values" Index, I show that one third of working respondents are motivated intrinsically by their job--valuing their role for its own sake. Nearly one quarter are driven by social and community-related aspects of their employment, 17% by social status, and just over one quarter by the transactional financial benefits of their job. Although a majority of people would leave their role if offered their current salary as a guaranteed income, one fifth of workers would stay even if offered up to 120% of their salary. Intrinsically motivated workers were disproportionately likely to refuse a basic income at any substitution level. Groups attached to their job for non-monetary reasons were also more likely to pursue volunteering or work-like activities if they received guaranteed income substitution but could no longer perform their role. Crucially, these non-monetary work motivations are evenly distributed across the income distribution and between white- and blue-collar workers. I argue that these findings have implications for managing the AI transition, understanding attitudes to AI, and making sense of policy preferences. Guaranteeing a basic income may indeed be necessary for managing any future AI labor shock, yet it could ultimately fail to compensate workers for any loss of the non-monetary benefits they derive from work.
item.dc:creator: Julian Jacobs

item.title: Did the energy crisis turn borrowers green? Zonal power prices and green bond choice on Oslo B{\o}rs
item.description: arXiv:2610.39843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The energy crisis of 2021 to 2023 caused a sharp increase in Nordic electricity prices, with substantial differences across bidding zones. We use this variation to examine whether issuers exposed to higher local electricity prices were more likely to choose green bonds over conventional bonds. We construct a dataset of bonds listed on Oslo B{\o}rs between 2019 and 2025 by combining ESMA FIRDS reference data, including matured bonds, with Euronext green bond classifications and issuer registry information. We then match issuers to their electricity bidding zones and examine the relationship between local power prices and green bond choice using issuer and quarter fixed effects. The share of green bonds among new listings increased from 15% in 2019 to 48% in 2024, but we find no statistically significant evidence that higher local electricity prices increased the likelihood of green bond issuance. This finding is consistent across price exposure windows of three to twelve months and for both utilities and other issuers. However, the estimates rely on 21 identifying issuers, and the minimum detectable effect at 80% statistical power is 3.1 percentage points for a 10 EUR/MWh increase in electricity prices, meaning that smaller effects cannot be ruled out. The estimated effect is larger but imprecise among issuers with an earlier green bond, which implies an existing framework. We also find no clear association between carbon prices and green bond choice, although this analysis covers only eight utilities. Overall, the findings suggest that the growth of green bond issuance in Norway was more closely associated with broader market trends than with differences in local electricity prices.
item.dc:creator: My Thi Diem Phan, Tuyen Trung Truong, Hoai Phuong Ha, Dat Thanh Nguyen

item.title: When are complements and substitutes dual?
item.description: arXiv:2610.39844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For binary-action games on bipartite networks, strategic complements and strategic substitutes are one and the same: each can be transformed into the other by relabelling the actions of every player on exactly one side. In this note, I show that bipartiteness is necessary and sufficient for such a relabelling; as a consequence, bipartite networks are precisely those on which every binary-action game with strategic substitutes must have a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.
item.dc:creator: Philip R. Neary

item.title: A Proof for Generalized Egalitarianism
item.description: arXiv:2610.40312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proves a rigidity theorem characterizing the Gini-type Lorenz-area ordering under general decision-theoretic constraints together with weak Lorenz dominance, thereby resolving the characterization problem pursued in this line of research on egalitarianism. This does not, of course, bring the broader inquiry to an end. In a certain sense, it may instead mark a step beyond the infancy of our attempt to connect social choice theory, welfare economics, and formal moral philosophy through a common mathematical language. The main proof strategy was originally obtained by the author's own hand, though 5.6sol and Astra could effortlessly reproduce it without any additional hint.
item.dc:creator: Wei ShuAng

item.title: When Does Storage Complement Solar? Investment and Cost Recovery under Advanced Net Metering
item.description: arXiv:2610.40650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine the joint PV and storage operational and investment decisions of a prosumer under net energy metering (NEM) and peak/off-peak tariffs. Legacy NEM compensates net exports at the retail rate over a netting period, typically under time-invariant pricing. To better reflect system costs, tariff features are being reconsidered, with many U.S. states adopting time-varying prices and export compensation below the retail price. We formulate the prosumer decision problem as a cost minimization problem with charge/discharge, PV investment, and storage investment decisions. We analytically derive the optimal decisions based on the tariff's membership in one of six regions that partition the tariff space. Using these solutions, we examine the relationship between PV and storage, identifying when they are complements or substitutes. Furthermore, we identify the relationship between private DER incentives and the distribution utility's (DU's) net cost of serving the prosumer. For both storage and PV, when investment costs are greater than the costs of serving the customer, there is no tariff where investment in PV and storage decrease non-adopter bills. Under the same conditions, complementarity between PV and storage decreases DU cost recovery for a given tariff. In a Massachusetts-based case study, we validate our theoretical findings by connecting tariff design features to DER interaction, the DU's net cost, and DER adoption in a stochastic, multi-prosumer, and multi-period setting.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Engelman Lado, Ahmed Alahmed, Audun Botterud, Saurabh Amin

item.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
item.description: arXiv:2610.40324v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: People increasingly share personal goals online and invite others to forecast them. Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person's behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures ("Will I ...?"), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market's first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%. Crowds believe in the futures people pose for themselves, and the information that would correct them lies with the person.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu

item.title: Tracks to Modernity: Railroads, Growth, and Civic Institutions in Denmark
item.description: arXiv:2502.21141v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We examine how railroads shaped Denmark's nineteenth-century economic transformation and the diffusion of Grundtvigian institutions. Using a panel of 1589 parishes and a difference-in-differences design for staggered adoption, we find that railroad connection increased local population by 7 percent, partly through internal in-migration, and structural change away from agriculture. Railroad access also brought cultural and institutional change by increasing the local densities of folk high schools and community houses, though these results are less robust than the economic findings.
item.dc:creator: Tom G\"orges, Magnus {\O}rberg Rove, Paul Sharp, Christian Vedel

item.title: Learning to Detect Recessions from Pseudo-out-of-sample Tests
item.description: arXiv:2506.09664v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Everyone is keen to know when a recession has started, but official announcements come only after several months, and real-time detection methods typically struggle---as the Great Recession showed. These methods face two challenges. First, they rely on data that are later significantly revised (such as GDP), so they only have a muddied view of the situation in real time. Second, they optimize in-sample performance, but this does not guarantee out-of-sample results. This paper proposes an algorithm that addresses both. First, it detects recessions from data on labor market slack---unemployment and vacancy rates---which are barely revised. Second, it selects recession classifiers for out-of-sample performance, using pseudo-out-of-sample tests on past recessions. Placed in the shoes of the NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee, the algorithm issues an early warning 5.2 months before the NBER announcement on average over the 6 recessions since 1978, and it reaches a 100% recession probability before the announcement or in the same month in 5 of them. The algorithm produces only one false positive out of sample: it takes the 2023--2024 labor market slowdown for a recession. Trained on the data between April 1929 and December 2025, the algorithm gives a recession probability of 0% in August 2026.
item.dc:creator: Pascal Michaillat

item.title: The Costs of Early-career Disciplinary Pivots: Evidence from Ph.D. Admissions
item.description: arXiv:2603.22805v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Science often advances when researchers pivot from one discipline to another and import new ideas. However, for established researchers, such pivots are associated with fewer publications and citations. Here, we investigate pivoting at the beginning of a research career--doctoral admissions--when the benefits of importing ideas might outweigh the switching costs. Analyzing 171,347 PhD applications at a large research university from 2013 to 2023, we measured the semantic distance between each applicant's prior degree and target program. Applicants who pivot further had lower undergraduate grades and, controlling for academic and demographic predictors, lower admission chances: the average pivot corresponds to a 5.3% lower admission probability (0.80 percentage points). Among enrollees, the average pivoter takes longer to graduate than non-pivoters, with a 10.7% lower graduation hazard, and similar publication and citation counts on average and at the tails. Our results suggest that pivoting at the outset of research careers, even if it benefits research communities, comes with significant costs to individuals.
item.dc:creator: Sidney Xiang, Nicholas David, Dallas Card, Wenhao Sun, Daniel M Romero, Misha Teplitskiy

item.title: How Firms Export: An Assignment Theory of Export Organization
item.description: arXiv:2606.18684v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a model in which direct exporters, indirect exporters, pure intermediaries, and hybrid exporters emerge endogenously from the assignment of products to export platforms. Firms differ in manufacturing and commercial capabilities. Manufacturing capability determines a product's potential profitability, while commercial capability determines how effectively a platform can sell it abroad. Manufacturing activation and product assignments are jointly determined, subject to fixed manufacturing costs, contracting frictions, and increasing organizational costs. Complementarity between manufacturing and commercial capabilities generates positive assortative matching, while organizational diseconomies shape platform scope. Equilibrium allocations can feature manufacturers exporting through their own platforms or those of other firms, specialized intermediaries exporting products they do not manufacture, and hybrid firms exporting their own products alongside those manufactured by other firms. The model characterizes how contracting costs, foreign-market attractiveness, and organizational diseconomies affect equilibrium assignments.
item.dc:creator: Asier Minondo

item.title: Whom Do AI Agents Serve? Role-Induced Sponsorship Bias in Decision Models and Generative LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2609.17989v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consumers increasingly delegate product search to AI shopping agents powered either by generative large language models (LLMs) that deliberate in natural language or by non-generative decision models that output calibrated choice probabilities in a single forward pass. Because retail platforms monetize through sponsored placements that shoppers typically discount, we examine whether an AI agent's evaluation of paid listings depends on who delegates the agent across both model families. Across three studies with no instructions to favor advertisers, naming a booking platform (vs. a traveler) as the agent's principal significantly attenuates the penalty applied to sponsored listings. Study 1 establishes this sponsorship bias across generative LLMs, prompt wordings, and reasoning efforts, showing that platform delegation weakens pre-choice skepticism and that naming the consumer as the beneficiary eliminates the bias. Study 2 establishes the bias across six commercial and open-weight decision models on calibrated choice probabilities and shows that consumer-aligned fine-tuning of an open-weight decision model (Kev 9B) across non-hotel retail categories eliminates the bias zero-shot on hotel choices. Study 3 decomposes the disclosure label across both model families, showing that attributing the placement to the platform triggers the sponsorship bias, whereas stricter disclosure wording ("Sponsored" vs. "Promoted") lowers paid-listing evaluation without eliminating this bias.
item.dc:creator: Davood Wadi, Yu Ma

item.title: The missing price feedback: Why studies overstate local grid peaks from synchronized home batteries under real-time pricing
item.description: arXiv:2609.35111v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing studies consistently find that home batteries optimized against real-time electricity prices create new load peaks in local distribution grids. This is because all assets respond to the same price signal in sync. However, most of these studies are simulations, and they all treat wholesale prices as exogenous, i.e., unaffected by the battery dispatch. This paper argues that assuming prices to be non-responsive biases the result: in reality, charging in low-price hours raises the wholesale price, which dampens the incentive to charge. In equilibrium, charging is spread out across hours. I test this by simulating households with rooftop solar and home batteries under a spot-based retail tariff with a model of equilibrium wholesale prices, calibrated to German data for 2025. With exogenous prices, my results confirm the literature findings: synchronous charging pushes the coincident import peak of the local grid to 83 % above its no-battery level. With endogenous prices, the same fleet leaves the peak 6 % below the no-battery benchmark. This finding is robust across alternative price functions and exogenous price paths, different measures of the coincident peak, 22 scenario variations and three historical years. I conclude that while new local peaks remain possible, particularly in grids that contain local clusters of home batteries, the risk and magnitude are considerably smaller than the existing literature suggests.
item.dc:creator: Lion Hirth

item.title: Strategic Integration of Artificial Intelligence in the C-Suite: The Role of the Chief AI Officer
item.description: arXiv:2407.10247v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into corporate strategy has become critical for organizations seeking to maintain competitive advantage in the digital age. Although organizations increasingly rely on AI as a strategic and organizational resource, existing C-suite roles remain only partially equipped to govern, integrate, and leverage it coherently at the enterprise level. Organizations vary in their responses. Some create a dedicated Chief AI Officer (CAIO), others extend existing mandates into hybrid roles, and still others coordinate AI through federated structures. This paper develops a role-design theory to explain this variation. I identify three properties that distinguish AI systems from earlier cross-cutting enterprise technologies, distributed accountability for judgment, upstream governance, and non-stationarity, and three configurations through which organizations respond: concentrated extension, distributed extension, and role creation. Four propositions specify when a dedicated CAIO emerges, what form an organization's response takes, when the role is effective, and how configurations evolve. Drawing on the first archival census of executive AI leadership, I find that the role has diffused sharply since 2023, that role creation and mandate extension are advancing in near parity, that adoption concentrates where digital leadership structures already exist, and that executive tenures contradict practitioner accounts of a transient role. The paper contributes to research on executive leadership, AI governance, and the design of AI-driven organizations.
item.dc:creator: Marc Schmitt

item.title: MOE-DGSCND: Multi-Objective Enterprise Green Supply Chain Network Design
item.description: arXiv:2609.11971v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper introduces and studies the Multi-Objective Enterprise Doubly-Green Supply Chain Network Design (MOE-DGSCND) problem, an extension of Multi-Objective Supply Chain Network Design. The problem studied here is a three-objective combinatorial optimization problem that simultaneously minimizes total cost f1, carbon dioxide emissions f2 and customer dissatisfaction f3 over binary decisions regarding which distribution centers to open and how to assign customer zones to open facilities. The problem generalizes the capacitated facility location problem (CFLP) and is known to be NP-hard (Garey and Johnson, 1979). This paper formally specifies the decision variables, objective functions and constraints and investigates three solution approaches using a single numerical instance: (A) an exact weighted-sum integer linear programming (ILP) formulation solved with Python combinatorially and via PuLP, (B) three Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Schemes (FPTAS) providing (1 + $\epsilon$)-approximate solutions for $\epsilon$ := 0.15 and (C) two baseline heuristics for comparison. On an instance with eight customers and five candidate distribution centers, the exact solver certifies the optimal (sampled) supported solutions across eight weight combinations, while the FPTAS-based approaches complete within milliseconds, compared to centiseconds for the exact ILP on this tiny non-stochastic instance.
item.dc:creator: Felix Reichel
